Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand how mothers are feeling emotionally in the first months after having a baby.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; nothing is shared beyond that without your permission. My goal is to create a comfortable, judgment-free space so we can best support you. The questions ask about the past seven days, and we’ll move through them one by one.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can start. Here’s the first question:  

Looking back over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Yeah… most of the time I can still laugh. My husband will say something goofy while we’re changing diapers and I’ll catch myself giggling. It’s not quite as easy as before the baby, but funny moments still get through.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly, yeah. I still laugh—like when my husband makes goofy faces at the baby—but it feels a little dimmer, like I have to remind myself to enjoy it instead of it just happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes… I’ll think, “Oh, it’ll be nice to take the baby for a walk tomorrow,” but when the time comes I’m kind of dragging my feet. I still want to do stuff, just not with the same excitement I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that. Like, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I’ll catch myself thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—other moms seem to calm their babies faster.” It’s not every minute, but it pops up a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit. Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby isn’t breathing—even when he’s right there in my arms and clearly fine. It only lasts a minute or two, then I can talk myself down, but it keeps catching me off-guard.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more like a quick flutter of “what if something bad happens?” It passes fast and I can settle myself, so I wouldn’t call it scared, just on-edge for a moment.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like yesterday—laundry piled up, the baby wanted to nurse every hour, and I felt as if I couldn’t get one thing finished before the next started. I manage, but it feels as though I’m running just to stay in place.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, it’s not that bad. I do get sad once in a while, but I still fall asleep pretty easily—maybe just lie there an extra ten minutes if the baby’s been extra fussy that day.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… I’ve had moments of feeling down, mostly when I’m alone during the baby’s nap. It’s not all day, but a couple of times this week I just felt heavy and weepy for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I did cry—twice this week. Once when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing him, and again when my mom left after visiting. It wasn’t sobbing all day, just tears that came and went.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’d never want to hurt myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Identified symptoms / concerns**
- Diminished ability to enjoy activities (laughing, outings) – present but still situational  
- Persistent self-blame and guilt over routine infant-care challenges  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries about infant safety without objective trigger  
- Episodic sadness, “heavy/weepy” mood, and isolated crying spells (2× this week)  
- Periodic sense of being overwhelmed; difficulty staying ahead of daily tasks  
- Denies thoughts of self-harm; no panic-level episodes

**Pattern summary**
Mood: mild–moderate anhedonia and lability, with intermittent tearfulness.  
Anxiety: low-grade, situational worries; no avoidance or physiologic panic.  
Functioning: managing basic care, but perceives effort as “running to stay in place.”  
Sleep: intact except for brief latency increases linked to situational stress, not primary mood-related insomnia.

**Screening relevance**
Findings are below diagnostic threshold for major postpartum depression but exceed “baby-blues” parameters; possible subsyndromal / emerging postpartum depressive/anxiety features warrant continued monitoring, psychoeducation, and formal follow-up (e.g., PHQ-9, GAD-7, or clinician interview) within 2–4 weeks or sooner if symptoms intensify, enjoyment further declines, or self-harm ideation emerges.
